review_shortlist.review_prompt: LOOK HERE FIRST: Inspect the head: outer sterile florets are enlarged and trumpet-like with fringed tips, surrounding shorter central fertile florets. Then turn the head sideways to inspect several rows of non-spiny green phyllaries with dark or pale papery fringed appendages. Ch
Bushy submerged watermilfoil with feather-like whorled leaves and emergent flowering shoots that transition to broader serrate bracts.

Go straight to the giant velvety leaves and mature fruit. Velvetleaf has a large ~15 × 20 mm schizocarp forming a conspicuous crown of mericarps with 3–6 mm divergent spines; the style is 13–15-branched.
Inspect white-tomentose stems and broad opposite leaves; then large rose-purple umbels and the conspicuously star-like individual flowers, hoods and horns.
Wetland grass with very rough cutting leaf margins and an open panicle of flattened one-flowered spikelets resembling tiny rice grains.
Inspect large oval leaves with rounded chestnut-like teeth and dense grayish pubescence beneath; then check the large acorn seated in a shallow cup.

Inspect several mature leaves from one branch: water oak commonly has a narrow wedge-shaped base and a broader, often shallowly three-lobed bristle-tipped apex. Confirm small second-year acorns in shallow cups.
Check the leaves first: willow oak has long, narrow, unlobed willow-like blades with smooth margins and a tiny terminal bristle. Then check the small acorns in shallow saucer-like cups.

Look at the basal leaves first: huge, stiff, deeply pinnatifid blades cut almost to the midrib into narrow lobes. Then check the towering flowering stem and yellow ray-and-disk heads. Leaf north-south orientation is variable and not diagnostic by itself.
Start with leaf arrangement and head type: alternate, resinous/gland-dotted, usually petiolate leaves below a rounded cluster of many tiny pink-purple heads with no ray florets.

Check red to scarlet reflexed corolla lobes around bright yellow or orange-yellow corona hoods, then inspect the opposite, relatively smooth narrow leaves. Verify the milky latex and erect, often branched habit. Contrast with native butterfly milkweed, which has alternate hairy l

Start with where the flowers are. Common wild petunia sends a conspicuous peduncled, branching terminal flower stalk above the leaves; the flowers are not sitting directly in the leaf axils. Then confirm mostly glabrous/glabrescent oval-ovate leaves with wavy to low-dentate margi
Rounded lobes, light gray scaly bark, shallow unfringed acorn cups.
Tall colonial bulrush with soft round culms and a lateral-looking cluster of drooping spikelets beneath a short continuation bract.

TRUE eastern annual saltmarsh aster under the narrow modern Texas concept: first photograph the ENTIRE flowering array on an unmowed mature plant. S. subulatum typically concentrates more heads in an upper, denser PYRAMID, whereas inland S. divaricatum is conspicuously DIFFUSE wi

Start with the long naked flower stalk and perfume. Fragrant gaillardia is a taprooted perennial with a basal rosette, very long mostly leafless peduncles, fragrant heads, and rays that may be tiny or completely absent, leaving a pincushion-like purple-brown disk.
Look at texture before color: this is an herbaceous perennial with conspicuously silky few-foliolate leaves and a densely white-villous, fuzzy conic-to-cylindrical flower head.
Look for narrow linear leaflets plus a dense swollen cylindrical-to-ovoid head. If the real question is D. compacta versus D. purpurea, move immediately to the calyx.

LOOK AT A MATURE LEAF: low or pink mock vervain has small, broadly ovate-to-triangular leaves (ca. 12–27 mm) with 3–6 pairs of comparatively broad fan-shaped primary lobes, often with secondary notches. Then inspect the very small flowers and the terminal spike: even in FRUIT the

Compare the flower and fruit together: this annual has a mostly glabrous flowering spike with white 12–19 mm four-petaled flowers, crimson anthers, and a short chunky nutlike fruit with four major lobes/ridges.

more_review_candidates.review_prompt: Start with the leaves: most are conspicuously 3-lobed or deeply cut, with a long central lobe and smaller lateral lobes; then notice the coarse hispid/glandular plant and multiple terminal or axillary spikes.
Look at spacing along the spike: flowers and broad bracts are visibly separated along a long slender, often nodding or drooping rachis rather than packed into a dense head.

Start with the tiny wiry reddish plant and narrow appressed seedhead branches. Red grama is a short perennial bunchgrass with very narrow mostly basal leaves and 2–7 small persistent red to purplish pectinate branches held close to the main axis.
Start with life cycle and the upper sheaths. Poverty dropseed is an annual, usually much smaller than perennial dropseeds, and it produces cleistogamous flowers hidden in the upper leaf sheaths.

Start with the smooth-looking green compound leaves and upright woody shrub habit. Roemer's false indigo has pinnate leaves with relatively large mostly glabrous leaflets and terminal purple flower racemes that rise above the foliage.

Start with the leaves and flower spikes. Hall's prairie clover is a slender perennial with mostly 3-foliolate leaves, sparse wiry stems, and relatively loose spikes of conspicuous yellow flowers. The calyx ribs/teeth are often reddish-brown and hairy.
Look at the deep acorn cup that almost encloses the nut; then examine rounded leaf lobes and pale hairy undersides.

LOOK FIRST at stem HAI​RS and panicle shape, not dry habitat: Julia's goldenrod has an evenly white-soft-hairy (densely villoso-tomentose) stem, narrow 3-nerved middle leaves often 5–10 mm wide with moderately dense fine hairs, and a LONG NARROW pyramid-like branching panicle abo

Find an areole before anything else. On the flattened green cladodes, each areole is a specialized short shoot that can carry hairs, glochids, permanent spines, flowers, or new pads. Then compare pad shape, spine/glochid pattern, yellow-to-orange flower, and beet-red berry.

needs_more_source_photos.review_prompt: Start with the woody shrub habit and long red-orange tubular flowers. Flame acanthus is a many-stemmed deciduous shrub with opposite narrow leaves and terminal clusters of narrow two-lipped hummingbird flowers.
Tall nearly glabrous dioecious amaranth with long-petioled leaves and long terminal spikes; pistillate plants have sharp bracts longer than the tepals.
Small annual amaranth with mostly axillary congested flower clusters rather than a big terminal spike, and relatively small ovate-to-rhombic leaves.
Robust upright pigweed with a reddish lower stem, obvious soft hairs on the upper stem and branches, and a short thick terminal green flower spike.
Low annual with axillary flower clusters from base to top; the cluster axes become thick, inflated and hard at maturity, with uniquely keeled flower bracts.
Bushy upright amaranth with the easiest character in the genus: a pair of sharp spines at nearly every leaf node.
Smooth green annual with slender terminal spikes, rounded or notched leaf tips, only three tepals, and a small indehiscent rugose fruit.
Look for alternate pinnate leaves bearing multiple pointed leaflets, red-to-blue small drupes in clusters and smooth gray bark on young trunks.
Start with the compound leaf: many narrow lance-shaped leaflets sit along a conspicuously winged rachis. Then confirm the deciduous, clonal shrub/small-tree habit and vivid red fall color.
Slender finely dissected ferny leaves and very small white flowers in compound umbels; look closely at the tiny ribbed two-part fruits.
Small woodland herb with palmately divided leaves and inconspicuous greenish flowers in tight umbels; inspect hooked bristly fruit.

Look for a low, densely hairy plant with dark maroon-to-brown star-shaped flowers, commonly paired close to the stem and heart-shaped leaves. Then inspect the milkweed gynostegium in the flower center.
Look for a vigorous twining vine with large opposite cordate leaves, relatively large uniform olive-green star-shaped flowers, and a long smooth follicle with strong longitudinal angles.

Like Texas snakeweed, an open and wispy yellow-flowering annual. Examine the back of a real flower head: pale/resinous phyllaries without green midnerve borders; then the DISC floret has long white basally united pappus scales, unlike G. texana's nearly absent/very short scales.
Inspect small white-ray daisy heads on finely branched stems; examine narrow leaf blades, disc florets and phyllaries.
Inspect a yellow composite flower head surrounded by narrow phyllaries ending in sharp spines; look for winged stem portions.
Inspect wiry branching stems with very narrow leaves and small yellow all-ray flower heads; basal foliage can be lobed.

Inspect the UPPER (adaxial) surface of a mature leaf with a hand lens. Bull thistle has numerous short appressed BRISTLELIKE SPINES projecting from the BLADE, not only spines at the margins. Also check the strongly decurrent leaf bases forming long spiny stem wings. This combinat
Shiny leaves with prominent white marbled veins and stiff marginal spines; purple heads with long spine-tipped phyllaries.
Mat-forming creeping plant with opposite thickened leaves that may be three-lobed and solitary yellow daisy-like heads; inspect rooting nodes.

START by checking the many short, stiff, narrow branchlet leaves and crowded small pale heads. With a 10–20× hand lens, turn a mature head sideways and seek the tiny actual WHITE/CLEAR terminal spine on the OUTER PHYLLARY (involucral bract). The bract bases may look whitish/paper
Expect an intermediate ironweed. Plants occur where western ironweed and woolly ironweed meet, with foliage, hairiness, leaf width, and head characters falling between the parents.
Inspect the shrub's multiple-compound leaves, white flowers in large sprays and clusters of persistent red berries.
Inspect softly hairy, elongated leaves, coiled flower branches, and the prickly, four-part fruit that catches on clothing.
Inspect four yellow petals in a cross, basal deeply lobed leaves, and slender siliques (seedpods) on ascending stalks.
Yellow-flowered bladderpod whose upper leaves are notably sessile, helping separate it from more obviously petiolate relatives.
Observe small four-petaled yellow mustard flowers and distinctly two-parted fruit with a swollen upper segment; inspect leaves and fruiting stems.
Highly branched mustard with deeply divided lower leaves, tiny four-petaled yellow flowers and long slender siliques.
Opposite, oval leaves and clusters of five-petaled pink or white flowers above a long tube-shaped calyx.
Inspect opposite narrow leaves, slender upright branches, small pink five-petaled flowers and a sticky band beneath the upper stem nodes.

Look for a sprawling or twining vine with thickened storage roots and highly variable heart-shaped to deeply lobed leaves. Flowers, when present, are pale pink to lavender morning-glory funnels with a darker throat.
Tiny tufted wet-ground sedge with narrow nearly leafless culms; inspect solitary terminal spikelet, dark scales and mature achenes.
Small tufted sedge with mostly leafless round stems, each topped by a solitary compact spikelet; inspect achene and bristle features.
Tufted wetland sedge with round leafless stems and one narrow spikelet per culm; confirm via tubercle, bristles and achene surfaces.
Wetland perennial with slender stems and one terminal spikelet; inspect stiff bent or rooting culms and the long-beaked achene tubercle.
Start with leaf size, bark, and ripe fruit: much larger leaves than Texas persimmon, dark blocky/checkered mature bark, and yellow-orange to reddish ripe fruit rather than black.
Inspect narrow silvery-scaled leaves, silvery twigs, small yellowish fragrant tubular flowers, and olive-like fruits.
Texas annual milkvetch in the Nuttallianus complex with 4–12 flowers per raceme, relatively broad leaflets, and long narrow glabrous pods.
Inspect leaves in groups of three leaflets, branched racemes of small pink pea flowers and jointed pods that break into flat segments.
Low spreading annual legume with leaves of three small leaflets, inconspicuous pinkish pea flowers and flattened one-seeded pods.
Inspect three-toothed leaflets and an elongate raceme of tiny white pea flowers; look for small pods developing along the raceme.
Inspect toothed leaflets in groups of three, narrow clusters of tiny yellow pea-flowers and the developing legume pods.

Find one complete compound leaf and count leaflet pairs: about 4–8 pairs of oval-to-oblong, softly hairy leaflets, versus the SINGLE pair in S. roemeriana and S. pilosior. Verify velvety upper and lower surfaces and the deep-rooted erect perennial habit; use flowers and mature po
Inspect whorls of finely feather-divided leaves around emergent aquatic stems; compare the aerial and submerged growth.
Inspect opposite, strongly toothed aromatic leaves on a square stem, and the small two-lipped flowers arranged in slender spikes.
Small wet-ground herb with opposite narrow leaves, four-parted tiny flowers in leaf axils and capsule fruits; inspect flower calyx close up.

Nonlocal A. incanum comparison: 5 style/stigma branches and about 5 mature fruit segments, often dark-centered reflexed corolla. FNA does not place the species in Texas; a Hays identification merits comparison with A. fruticosum. Do not rely on staminal-column hair alone; A. frut

Start with life form and the underside of the flower. Tall poppymallow is an annual (sometimes biennial) with one to several erect/weakly erect stems and NO involucellar bractlets beneath the calyx. In bud the calyx lobes meet valvately to form a pointed tip.
Smooth green young branches and very large palmately lobed leaves; look for open boat-shaped fruit follicles carrying exposed seeds.
Inspect round to shallowly lobed, scalloped leaves and the small pale flowers clustered at leaf axils; confirm the segmented disk-shaped fruit.
Inspect opposite leaves, clustered small pink flowers held in bract-like involucres and the dark, ribbed mature anthocarps.

Once you know it is an ash, go to the lower leaflet surface and the samara: Texas ash usually has a glaucous white-reticulate waxy underside, a relatively small seed body, and a wing that is terminal or only slightly decurrent.

Look at the samara first: green ash has a larger seed body with the wing decurrent well down the body before broadening; then confirm a broad shield-shaped leaf scar and usually non-glaucous lower leaflet surface.

Both this species and Ludwigia repens have opposite leaves on creeping stems. Find an axillary flower: palustris has four green sepals and no yellow petals. Do not rely only on absent petals because repens may be apetalous or shed petals. Check the ovary/mature capsule: palustris

Inspect opposite paired leaves along a creeping, node-rooting stem. Look for very small yellow petals (when present), but note they may be shed or naturally absent. Crucially, a mature capsule lacks the four dark-green longitudinal bands seen on L. palustris. Do not force submerg
Leafless mycoheterotrophic orchid with thin pale to reddish stems and small orchid flowers; examine labellum patterns and floral spurs.
Slender herb with opposite narrow leaves and an elongated spike of violet-blue tubular flowers; inspect four-lobed corollas and bracts.
Inspect hairy stems with lobed leaves and a rounded seed capsule capped by a radiating, disk-like stigma.
Inspect very large opposite heart-shaped leaves, pale lavender tubular flowers and brown woody egg-shaped seed capsules.
Low spreading perennial with oval leaves and terminal clusters of five-lobed bright blue flowers; inspect tubular calyces and flower bases.

Start with the fluffy head. Bushy bluestem makes dense broomlike to cottony clusters near the top of the plant, with paired short rames packed inside and emerging from upper leaf sheaths. The inflorescence looks bushy rather than like separate turkey-foot fingers.

Look at the number and shape of the flowering branches: blue grama usually has 1–3 conspicuous unilateral racemes shaped like curved eyebrows or rooster combs, with spikelets packed all the way to the branch tip.

Think intermediate between Lindheimer muhly and seep muhly: a dense upright perennial bunchgrass with firm folded leaves and an open erect panicle, usually in rocky canyons and prairie openings where the parent ranges overlap.
Dense soft fuzzy bottlebrush-like flower panicle, formed by numerous long awns on closely packed spikelets.
Long, narrow terminal cereal spike with rows of overlapping spikelets bearing long awns; inspect the glumes and lemma tips.

Start at the collar and then the seedhead. Indiangrass is a tall warm-season perennial with a conspicuous stiff membranous ligule and auricle-like collar extensions, plus a dense golden-bronze panicle with once-bent twisted awns.
Tall rhizomatous grass with broad blades bearing a conspicuous pale midrib; inspect open panicles, spikelets and ligule.
Small Texas fluffgrass relative with a compact seedhead and conspicuous cottony or fluffy hairs around the spikelets at maturity.
Inspect small opposite oval leaves and solitary five-lobed flowers on slender axillary stalks, with round capsules after flowering; flower color varies.
Early-flowering buttercup with divided basal foliage, several yellow glossy petals and rounded aggregates of small achenes.
Large yellow many-stamened flowers on herbaceous stems with lobed basal leaves; confirm petal size and mature achene head.
Inspect hairy stems and three-lobed lower leaves; small glossy yellow five-petaled flowers followed by a rounded head of achenes.
Moist-site herb with divided or lobed leaves, small yellow flowers and a long cylindrical cluster of many small achenes.
Inspect alternately arranged toothed leaves, thorny twigs, five-petaled white flowers and red pome fruits; verify against similar hawthorns.
Glossy, alternate oval leaves with finely toothed edges; clusters of five-petaled white flowers and small rounded fruits.
Woody arching stems with small narrow leaves and clusters of five-petaled white flowers borne along the twigs.
Low, trailing plant with leaves arranged in apparent whorls and tiny pink-purple four-lobed flowers in dense clusters.
Inspect compound or partially bipinnate leaves, large yellow flower panicles and inflated three-sided papery fruit capsules.
Inspect climbing fern fronds with finely divided, lace-like pinnae and distinctive spore-bearing lobes on fertile leaflets.
Climbing woody vine with tendrils arising near leaf stalks; inspect bristly or prickly stems, broad leaves and berries in umbels.
Evergreen or nearly evergreen shrub with alternate leathery entire leaves and fragrant pale flowers clustered along twigs; inspect leaf undersides and fruit.
Fine jointed green twigs with almost invisible sheathing scale leaves and small pale flowers in narrow racemes.

LOOK AT A MATURE LEAF: larger prairie verbena often has a fernlike outline with deeply once- or twice-divided blades and many narrow secondary lobes. Then compare terminal flower clusters and watch mature spikes elongate in fruit. Do not identify by pink-purple flower color alone

Look at the leaf dissection and overall slenderness first: lower leaves are often deeply pinnatifid, while the upper flowering branches become narrow and simple; the plant is much less gray-woolly than Verbena canescens.
